result: HyVL achieves millimeter-precision localization of ultrasonic vocalizations (3.4-4.8 mm MAE, 91% assignment rate), representing a ~3× improvement over previous methods. The system combines a 64-channel acoustic camera (Cam64) with four high-quality ultrasonic microphones (USM4), exploiting their complementary error patterns (L-shaped distribution) to achieve superior performance. This accuracy approaches the physical limits imposed by mouse snout dimensions (~10 mm).
evaluation: Claims C4, C28-C32, C50, C52-C58 provide convergent evidence from multiple experimental conditions (all USVs, far condition, single animal) showing consistent sub-centimeter accuracy. The complementary error patterns (C27, C46, C48-C49) and systematic comparison with previous methods (C30, C93-C95) strongly support the performance claims. The hybrid combination strategy (C47, C120-C121) is empirically justified through comparative testing.

result: The Cam64 MEMS microphones exhibit frequency-dependent noise characteristics with a rising noise floor at higher frequencies, limiting detection of very-high-frequency USVs, while USM4 microphones maintain flat baseline noise across the relevant frequency range.
evaluation: Claims C37-C41 are directly supported by spectral analysis data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, showing quantitative differences in noise characteristics between the two microphone systems. This technical characterization justifies the hybrid approach.

result: Males and females vocalize in spatially distinct positions during courtship: females vocalize almost exclusively during close snout-snout contact, while males vocalize both during snout-snout contact and when approaching the female ano-genital region. The fraction of female vocalizations (4.4% with MPI selection using HyVL) is significantly lower than previously estimated, suggesting prior overestimation due to imprecise localization.
evaluation: Claims C7, C62-C77 are supported by spatial analysis data (Figure 4F-I) and statistical comparisons between SLIM and HyVL (p=0.002, C64). The spatial positioning patterns (C71-C74) are quantitatively demonstrated. However, C77 acknowledges that close snout-snout contact has the highest misassignment risk, introducing some uncertainty about the remaining female vocalizations.

result: In competitive triadic interactions (two males, one female), one male takes a dominant role, vocalizing ~9× more than the subordinate male (p<0.005) and spending more time in ano-genital contact with the female. The subordinate male engages more in snout-snout interactions. Male mice approach females more closely during triadic versus dyadic trials (p=0.00046).
evaluation: Claims C9, C33, C80-C92 are supported by vocalization rate analysis (Figure 5A-B) and spatial interaction histograms (Figure 6A-D) with appropriate statistical testing including Bonferroni correction. The spatial differences are validated through bootstrapping (C90). The ~9-fold difference in vocalization rate is striking and well-documented.

result: In dyadic trials, no significant individual differences in vocalization rates were found for either male (p=0.46) or female (p=0.16) mice. Vocalization energy showed non-significant trends between dominant and submissive males in triadic pairings, with no effects in females.
evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by one-way ANOVA analysis on a balanced dataset (14×4 dyadic interactions, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Claims C83-C84 appropriately report non-significant trends. The statistical approach is appropriate for the experimental design.

result: Most USVs (93% in dyadic, 72% in triadic interactions) were emitted within 10 cm snout-snout distance, confirming that vocalizations occur predominantly during close-range social interactions.
evaluation: Claims C34-C36, C22 are directly supported by distance distribution data in Figure 1D. The quantitative percentages are clearly stated and visualized, providing strong evidence for the importance of high-precision localization during close interactions.

result: Automatic tracking using DeepLabCut (dyadic) and SLEAP (triadic) with custom post-processing achieved reliable tracking with minimal manual corrections (~10 per trial). Automatic tracking showed a median 3.76 mm difference from manual tracking, resulting in slightly increased localization error (~0.9 mm) but paradoxically higher assignment rates (93.6% vs 92%).
evaluation: Claims C167-C172 are supported by comparative analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, N=5046 USVs). The paradoxical increase in assignment rate with automatic tracking (C172) is noted but not fully explained, suggesting the automatic tracking may place snout markers slightly differently. The overall conclusion that automatic tracking is viable at slightly reduced accuracy is reasonable.

result: WT and KO (Foxp2flox/flox;Pcp2Cre) mice were pooled for analysis based on previous work and the authors' observations showing no differences in USV production between genotypes.
evaluation: Claim C140 cites previous work (Urbanus et al., 2020) and states the authors' own observations found no differences. However, no data is presented in this manuscript to support this claim. While the citation provides some support, the lack of presented data and the methodological focus of the work make this pooling decision uncertain. This could potentially confound results if subtle genotype differences exist.

result: Previous USV localization methods achieved progressively improving accuracy: Neunuebel et al. (2015) reported ~38 mm MAE (14.6-18.1% assignment), Warren et al. (2018a) achieved ~20-30 mm MAE (52-62% assignment), and Oliveira-Stahl et al. (2023) reached ~11-14 mm MAE (80-85% assignment).
evaluation: Claims C93-C95 accurately cite previous work and provide appropriate context for evaluating HyVL's performance. These are straightforward literature citations that establish the baseline for comparison.

result: Certain very close snout-snout interactions remain too close for reliable USV assignment. The mouse snout acts as a distributed sound source without a clear internal peak. Spectrally narrow USVs suffer from phase ambiguity, and acoustically occluded USVs have reduced SNR, with these issues affecting USM4 more than Cam64.
evaluation: Claims C115-C118, C124-C126 acknowledge system limitations based on observations from beamforming data (C116-C117) and acoustic principles (C124-C125). These are reasonable inferences about the physical and technical limits of the approach. The acknowledgment of limitations strengthens the overall credibility of the work.

result: Future improvements could include advanced acoustic modeling or deep learning to resolve close-interaction issues, improved USV detection/separation based on harmonic structure, and real-time localization via GPU streaming.
evaluation: Claims C119, C130-C132 are speculative suggestions for future work. While reasonable, they are not tested or validated in this manuscript. These represent potential directions rather than demonstrated capabilities.

result: Background context on USVs: they serve important roles in communication across species, have diverse functions, are context-dependent, and are increasingly used in neurodevelopmental research. Previous localization methods achieved 11-14 mm accuracy, insufficient for close snout-snout interactions where most USVs occur.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C10-C25, C59-C61, C101-C108 provide literature-based context supported by extensive citations. These establish the scientific rationale and prior state of the field. The claims are appropriately attributed to cited sources.

result: Detailed methodological descriptions of experimental setup, recording parameters, animal subjects, trial design, data preprocessing, USV detection, localization algorithms, assignment criteria, and statistical approaches.
evaluation: Claims C136-C189 provide comprehensive methodological details that are internally consistent and appropriately documented. The methods are sufficiently detailed for reproducibility. Ethical approval is documented (C136). Statistical methods are appropriate (nonparametric tests, C186-C189).

result: HyVL offers practical advantages including low cost (<€10k), ease of operation, compact form factor enabling home cage studies, and potential applicability to other species. The system could reduce animal numbers needed due to higher assignment rates.
evaluation: Claims C97, C99-C100, C109-C113, C134-C135 make assertions about cost, ease of use, and future applications that are partially speculative. While the cost estimate (C134) appears reasonable, claims about applicability to other species (C112-C113) and home cage studies (C109-C110) are not empirically validated in this work. The claim about reducing animal numbers (C135) is a logical inference but not directly demonstrated.

result: A small fraction of USVs (2.9%) were excluded due to the 50 mm proximity threshold. Very quiet, very short, or overlapping vocalizations (<0.1%) present detection and localization challenges, though overlaps were surprisingly rare.
evaluation: Claims C122-C123, C127-C129 provide quantitative data on system limitations and edge cases. The percentages are specific and the observations about overlapping vocalizations (C127-C129) are based on data analysis. These represent honest reporting of system limitations.
